title: Caribbean Kids Songs to Sing at Home
excerpt: Parents look for Caribbean kids songs that fit breakfast and bedtime. Here is what Likkle Radio actually plays, and how to use one short song without turning the day into a show.
content:
Parents search for Caribbean kids songs when they want the house to sound like home. That might be a short tune before school in London, a counting song in Toronto, or a food song in Port of Spain. The useful version is small. A child hears the islands in a familiar voice, and a parent does not have to build a music class from scratch.

What a short song can carry

One song can hold a word a child will use later: callaloo, doubles, coco water, soursop. It can also hold a feeling. Families in the diaspora often say the same thing. The child likes the tune. The parent hears something school playlists leave out.

For ages 3–9, one song at breakfast and one quieter song at night is enough. Little ones clap. Bigger ones can sing and then tell you what the food or place is. If your family uses a word the lyric does not have, keep that word. Caribbean English belongs in the room.

What Likkle Radio actually plays

Likkle Radio is free to listen to. No account is required. These are recorded songs from our library. It is not a live station, and it is not a promise that every Caribbean style is in the player.

Songs families use with little children include:

  • Island Alphabet and Island Counting, for letters and numbers
  • Callaloo, Doubles, Coco Water, and Soursop, for food words children already hear at home
  • Blue Mountain Coffee, a light Jamaica-flavored song
  • Island Shout Out and Island Shaped Song, for saying island names out loud
  • Island Lullaby and Goodnight Ocean Breeze, when the house needs to settle

Tanty Spice is the storyteller in this world. R.O.T.I. is the study buddy. Dilly Doubles is the hype-man friend. The play button is for a parent or a child together. Nobody in the kids portal is asked to pay for a song.

How to use a song without a performance

Press play while you do something you already do: pack a bag, stir a pot, or sit on the bed. Then ask one question. "What food was that?" or "Which island did we shout out?" Stop there. A quiz every morning makes the song feel like homework.

If a grandparent is on the phone, play ten seconds and ask whether they sang anything like it. That conversation does more for island pride than a worksheet.

What we will not pretend

These tracks do not replace a music teacher, a pan yard, or the songs your own family already owns. A child who skips a track is not less Caribbean. Try another one. Listening stays free on Likkle Radio even if you never open a paid parent plan.

When you want stories beside the music, a parent can start Free Forever. The free library rotates. It is not every story, forever, on day one. Children do not check out.
